title: Discrete Mathematics
subject: Mathematics

cards.prompt: Define alteration method. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The alteration method samples an object and then makes bounded repairs, controlling the expected final objective by the random defects removed or corrected.
required_concepts: The alteration method samples an object and then makes bounded repairs, controlling the expected final objective by the random defects removed or corrected.
major_error_concepts: Performing repairs without bounding their loss and then treating the original expectation as a guarantee for the altered object.

cards.prompt: How do big-O, big-Omega, and big-Theta differ?
cards.definition: **Definition.** For eventually nonnegative functions f and g, f=O(g) when f(n)<=C g(n) eventually for some C>0; f=Omega(g) when f(n)>=c g(n) eventually for some c>0; and f=Theta(g) when both bounds hold. Only mutual Theta comparison gives the usual asymptotic growth equivalence relation.
required_concepts: f=O(g) means f(n)<=C g(n) eventually for some C>0.
f=Omega(g) means f(n)>=c g(n) eventually for some c>0.
f=Theta(g) means both one-sided bounds hold.
Big-Theta, not one-sided big-O or big-Omega, gives the usual growth equivalence relation.
major_error_concepts: Calling one-sided big-O or big-Omega comparison an equivalence class, or dropping the eventual quantifier and positive constants.

cards.prompt: Define bijection principle. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** If there is a bijection between two finite sets, then they have the same cardinality, so either set may be counted by counting the other.
required_concepts: If there is a bijection between two finite sets, then they have the same cardinality, so either set may be counted by counting the other.
major_error_concepts: Using a mapping that is not both injective and surjective as a counting bijection.

cards.prompt: Define finite binary relation representation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A finite binary relation from A to B can be represented extensionally as its subset of A cross B, for example by a Boolean matrix or a directed incidence diagram; a relation on A uses A cross A.
required_concepts: The relation is represented as a subset of A cross B, or equivalently by finite incidence data with carriers A and B declared.
A relation on A uses A cross A.
major_error_concepts: Treating a finite relation's matrix or diagram as untyped data without declaring its row and column carrier sets.

cards.prompt: Define binomial coefficient. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The binomial coefficient C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n-k)!) counts k-element subsets of an n-element set for 0<=k<=n.
required_concepts: The binomial coefficient C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n-k)!) counts k-element subsets of an n-element set for 0<=k<=n.
major_error_concepts: Applying the factorial formula outside its declared integer range without an extension convention.

cards.prompt: What is binomial theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The binomial theorem identifies binomial coefficients as coefficients of a commutative two-term power and supplies identities by comparison or specialization; the usual formula does not directly apply to noncommuting factors.
required_concepts: It identifies binomial coefficients as the coefficients of a power of a two-term sum.
Algebraic comparison or specialization can yield counting identities.
Its usual form assumes the two terms commute.
major_error_concepts: Treating the theorem as a method for arbitrary noncommuting factors without qualification.

cards.prompt: State binomial theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For every nonnegative integer n, (x+y)^n=sum_{k=0}^n C(n,k)x^{n-k}y^k in any commutative ring where these expressions are defined.
required_concepts: For every nonnegative integer n, (x+y)^n=sum_{k=0}^n C(n,k)x^{n-k}y^k in any commutative ring where these expressions are defined.
major_error_concepts: Writing every coefficient as one, or using exponents whose sum is not n.

cards.prompt: Define bipartite graph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A graph is bipartite when its vertices can be partitioned into two sets so every edge has one endpoint in each set.
required_concepts: A graph is bipartite when its vertices can be partitioned into two sets so every edge has one endpoint in each set.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a graph is bipartite merely because it has two visibly dense regions.

cards.prompt: Define Boolean lattice. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The Boolean lattice B_n is the power set of an n-element set ordered by inclusion, with meet intersection and join union.
required_concepts: The Boolean lattice B_n is the power set of an n-element set ordered by inclusion, with meet intersection and join union.
major_error_concepts: Claiming an arbitrary finite lattice is a Boolean lattice B_n.

cards.prompt: Define bridge. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the number of connected components.
required_concepts: A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the number of connected components.
major_error_concepts: Calling every edge in a spanning tree a bridge of the original graph.

cards.prompt: Define characteristic polynomial of a recurrence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For a constant-coefficient homogeneous recurrence, the characteristic polynomial is obtained by substituting a trial solution r^n and collecting the resulting polynomial equation in r.
required_concepts: The recurrence is linear, homogeneous, and has constant coefficients.
Substituting the trial sequence r^n produces the polynomial equation whose left-hand side defines the characteristic polynomial.
major_error_concepts: Using a characteristic polynomial for a variable-coefficient recurrence without justification.

cards.prompt: Define chromatic number. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The chromatic number chi(G) is the minimum number of colors in a proper vertex coloring of G.
required_concepts: The chromatic number chi(G) is the minimum number of colors in a proper vertex coloring of G.
major_error_concepts: Reporting the number of colors in one coloring as the chromatic number without proving minimality.

cards.prompt: Define clique. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A clique is a vertex subset whose distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent.
required_concepts: A clique is a vertex subset whose distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent.
major_error_concepts: Calling a high-density subgraph a clique despite a missing pairwise edge.

cards.prompt: In a formal power series A(x), what does [x^n]A(x) denote?
cards.definition: **Definition.** The notation [x^n]A(x) denotes the coefficient of x^n in a formal power series A(x).
required_concepts: The notation [x^n]A(x) denotes the coefficient of x^n in a formal power series A(x).
major_error_concepts: Substituting a numerical x when the task is to extract a formal coefficient.

cards.prompt: Define combination. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A k-combination of an n-element set is an unordered k-element subset, for integers 0<=k<=n.
required_concepts: A k-combination is an unordered k-element subset of an n-element set.
The parameters satisfy integers 0<=k<=n.
major_error_concepts: Counting different orders of the same subset as distinct combinations.

cards.prompt: Define combinations with repetition. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For n>=1 types and r>=0 selections, the number of size-r multisets is binom(n+r-1,r).
required_concepts: The objects are size-r multisets chosen from n>=1 types, with r>=0.
Their number is binom(n+r-1,r).
major_error_concepts: Using binom(n+r-1,r) for ordered sequences rather than size-r multisets from n types.

cards.prompt: Define combinatorial invariant. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A combinatorial invariant is a quantity or property unchanged by the allowed transformations of a discrete object.
required_concepts: A combinatorial invariant is a quantity or property unchanged by the allowed transformations of a discrete object.
major_error_concepts: Calling a quantity invariant after checking only one transformation instance.

cards.prompt: Define connected component. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** In an undirected graph, a connected component is a maximal connected subgraph, equivalently an equivalence class of vertices under path reachability.
required_concepts: A connected component is a maximal connected subgraph, equivalently an equivalence class under reachability by paths.
major_error_concepts: Calling a connected subgraph a component when it is properly contained in a larger connected subgraph.

cards.prompt: Define connected graph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** An undirected graph is connected when every pair of vertices is joined by a path.
required_concepts: An undirected graph is connected when every pair of vertices is joined by a path.
major_error_concepts: Inferring connectedness from every vertex having positive degree.

cards.prompt: What does a finite-structure counterexample refute, and what makes a finite search exhaustive?
cards.definition: **Definition.** A finite-structure counterexample is one admissible assignment or object in the declared finite universe for which an imported universal claim fails; exhaustive finite search is sound only when it covers that whole universe.
required_concepts: The witness is admissible in the declared finite universe and makes the universal predicate false.
Finite search certifies absence or discovery only when it exhausts that declared universe.
major_error_concepts: Offering an object outside the declared finite universe, or calling a partial search exhaustive.

cards.prompt: Define cover relation in a poset. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** In a poset, y covers x when x<y and no z satisfies x<z<y.
required_concepts: In a poset, y covers x when x<y and no z satisfies x<z<y.
major_error_concepts: Claiming y covers x even though some z satisfies x<z<y.

cards.prompt: Define cycle. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** In a simple undirected graph, a cycle is a closed walk of length at least three whose vertices are distinct except for the common start and end.
required_concepts: The walk is closed and has length at least three.
No vertex repeats except the common start and end.
major_error_concepts: Calling any closed walk a cycle despite repeated internal vertices.

cards.prompt: What is derangement formula: role used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The formula is the standard inclusion-exclusion count for avoiding all fixed-point events; it does not assume those events are independent.
required_concepts: The formula is the standard inclusion-exclusion count for avoiding all fixed-point events
it does not assume those events are independent.
major_error_concepts: Deriving the formula by multiplying fixed-point avoidance probabilities as if those events were independent.

cards.prompt: State derangement formula: statement, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The number D_n of derangements of n objects is n! sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^j/j!, equivalently the nearest integer to n!/e for n>=1.
required_concepts: The number D_n of derangements of n objects is n! sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^j/j!, equivalently the nearest integer to n!/e for n>=1.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the alternating signs or the j! denominator, or using the nearest-integer form outside n>=1.

cards.prompt: Define derangement. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A derangement is a permutation with no fixed point.
required_concepts: A derangement is a permutation with no fixed point.
major_error_concepts: Calling a permutation a derangement when even one element remains in its original position.

cards.prompt: Define directed acyclic graph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a directed graph with no directed cycle.
required_concepts: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a directed graph with no directed cycle.
major_error_concepts: Treating absence of an undirected cycle as the definition, or overlooking a consistently oriented directed cycle.

cards.prompt: Define directed graph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A directed graph has vertices and ordered-pair edges, so adjacency has a direction.
required_concepts: A directed graph has vertices and ordered-pair edges, so adjacency has a direction.
major_error_concepts: Replacing ordered edge pairs by unordered pairs and thereby erasing edge direction.

cards.prompt: Define distributive lattice. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A distributive lattice is a lattice whose meet distributes over join and whose join distributes over meet.
required_concepts: A distributive lattice is a lattice whose meet distributes over join and whose join distributes over meet.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every lattice is distributive merely because joins and meets exist.

cards.prompt: Define divide-and-conquer recurrence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A divide-and-conquer recurrence models cost as the combined cost of recursive subproblems plus nonrecursive work, commonly T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n).
required_concepts: A divide-and-conquer recurrence models cost as the combined cost of recursive subproblems plus nonrecursive work, commonly T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n).
major_error_concepts: Writing a recurrence that ignores subproblem count, size, or combine work.

cards.prompt: Define double counting. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Double counting proves an identity by counting the same finite set of incidences or configurations in two different ways.
required_concepts: Double counting proves an identity by counting the same finite set of incidences or configurations in two different ways.
major_error_concepts: Counting two different underlying sets and equating the totals without a common carrier or bijection.

cards.term: Euler trail and circuit criterion: role
cards.prompt: What is Euler trail and circuit criterion used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The Euler criterion reduces an edge-covering traversal question to path connectivity among nonzero-degree vertices and degree parity; it says nothing about Hamilton paths or cycles, which ask to visit every vertex.
required_concepts: The criterion reduces edge-covering traversal existence to path connectivity among nonzero-degree vertices and degree parity.
It says nothing about Hamilton paths or cycles, which concern visiting every vertex rather than using every edge.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the criterion characterizes Hamilton cycles.

cards.term: Euler trail and circuit criterion: statement
cards.prompt: State Euler trail and circuit criterion, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** A finite undirected graph has an Euler circuit exactly when every two vertices of nonzero degree are joined by a path and every vertex has even degree. It has an open Euler trail exactly when every two vertices of nonzero degree are joined by a path and exactly two vertices have odd degree.
required_concepts: The graph is finite and undirected.
An Euler circuit exists exactly when every two nonzero-degree vertices are joined by a path and every vertex has even degree.
An open Euler trail exists exactly when every two nonzero-degree vertices are joined by a path and exactly two vertices have odd degree.
major_error_concepts: Applying only the degree-parity test when the nonisolated vertices lie in different components, or treating edge coverage as vertex coverage.

cards.prompt: What is Euler's planar formula: role used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** Euler's formula links local edge-face incidence to a global invariant and yields necessary nonplanarity bounds; satisfying a derived bound is not sufficient for planarity.
required_concepts: Euler's formula links local edge-face incidence to a global invariant and yields necessary nonplanarity bounds
satisfying a derived bound is not sufficient for planarity.
major_error_concepts: Treating a necessary edge bound derived from Euler's formula as a sufficient characterization of planarity.

cards.prompt: State Euler's planar formula: statement, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For a connected finite planar graph with a fixed planar embedding, V-E+F=2, where F includes the outer face.
required_concepts: For a connected finite planar graph with a fixed planar embedding, V-E+F=2, where F includes the outer face.
major_error_concepts: Using V-E+F=2 for a disconnected drawing without the component correction, or failing to count the outer face.

cards.prompt: How do an Euler trail and an Euler circuit differ?
cards.definition: **Definition.** In a finite undirected graph, an Euler trail is a trail that contains every edge exactly once, and an Euler circuit is an Euler trail whose initial and final vertices are the same.
required_concepts: The ambient graph is finite and undirected.
An Euler trail contains every edge exactly once.
An Euler circuit is an Euler trail with the same initial and final vertex.
major_error_concepts: Calling a vertex-covering Hamilton traversal Eulerian, allowing an edge to repeat, or calling an open Euler trail a circuit.

cards.term: existential quantification over a finite structure
cards.prompt: Define existential quantification over a finite structure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For a declared finite domain D, there exists x in D such that P(x) asserts that at least one member of D satisfies P and may be certified by one admissible witness.
required_concepts: The quantifier asserts that at least one member of the declared finite domain satisfies P.
One admissible member satisfying P is a witness.
major_error_concepts: Treating an existential witness as though it must be unique.

cards.prompt: What is expectation existence principle used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It turns an average-value calculation into an existence proof for at least one finite combinatorial object meeting the average threshold, which is the basic probabilistic-method move; it supplies no concentration or typicality claim.
required_concepts: It turns an average-value calculation into an existence proof for at least one finite combinatorial object meeting the average threshold, which is the basic probabilistic-method move
it supplies no concentration or typicality claim.
major_error_concepts: Concluding every outcome is close to the expectation.

cards.prompt: State expectation existence principle, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** If a real-valued statistic on a finite random object has expectation mu, then at least one outcome has value at least mu and at least one has value at most mu.
required_concepts: Hypotheses: If a real-valued statistic on a finite random object has expectation mu.
Conclusion: at least one outcome has value at least mu and at least one has value at most mu.
major_error_concepts: Concluding every outcome is close to the expectation.

cards.prompt: Define exponential generating function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The exponential generating function of (a_n) is sum_{n>=0} a_n x^n/n!, a normalization suited to many labeled combinatorial constructions.
required_concepts: The exponential generating function of (a_n) is sum_{n>=0} a_n x^n/n!, a normalization suited to many labeled combinatorial constructions.
major_error_concepts: Confusing its coefficients with those of the ordinary generating function by omitting n!.

cards.prompt: Define face of a planar embedding. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A face is a connected component of the plane after removing the drawing, including the unbounded outer face.
required_concepts: A face is a connected component of the plane after removing the drawing, including the unbounded outer face.
major_error_concepts: Counting only bounded regions and excluding the unbounded component, or defining faces without a fixed embedding.

cards.prompt: Define Finite expectation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For a real-valued random variable X on a finite probability space, E[X]=sum_{omega in Omega} X(omega)P({omega}), the probability-weighted average of its values.
required_concepts: E[X]=sum over omega in Omega of X(omega)P({omega}).
The weights are the declared outcome probabilities and sum to one.
major_error_concepts: Averaging outcome values uniformly when the outcomes are not equiprobable, or omitting an outcome with nonzero probability.

cards.prompt: Define finite graph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** This course's base finite graph G=(V,E) has a finite vertex set V and a finite edge collection E with a declared incidence rule. In a simple graph E can be a set of vertex pairs; multigraph multiplicity requires distinct edge objects or a multiplicity function.
required_concepts: V is finite and E is a finite edge collection with declared incidence.
A simple graph may encode edges as a set of vertex pairs.
Parallel edges require distinct edge objects or an explicit multiplicity function.
major_error_concepts: Using a bare set of endpoint pairs to claim two parallel edges, or leaving direction, loops, and multiplicity conventions undeclared.

cards.prompt: Define Finite indicator-count representation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For an event A in a finite probability space, 1_A(x)=1 iff x is in A (the event occurs), and 1_A(x)=0 otherwise. Thus for events A_1,...,A_m, the count N=sum_i 1_{A_i} satisfies E[N]=sum_i P(A_i), without independence.
required_concepts: The indicator 1_{A_i} equals one when A_i occurs and zero otherwise.
N=sum_i 1_{A_i} counts the occurring events.
E[N]=sum_i P(A_i) without an independence assumption.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the expected number of occurring events with the probability that at least one occurs, or requiring the events to be independent.

cards.prompt: Define finite linearity of expectation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For real-valued random variables X_1,...,X_m on one finite probability space, E[sum_i X_i]=sum_i E[X_i], by rearranging finite sums and without independence.
required_concepts: The finite family X_1,...,X_m is defined on one finite probability space.
E[sum_i X_i]=sum_i E[X_i] follows by rearranging finite sums.
No independence assumption is required.
major_error_concepts: Requiring independence for finite linearity or applying the identity to variables defined on different undeclared probability spaces.

cards.prompt: Define finite probability space. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A finite probability space assigns nonnegative probabilities summing to one to the outcomes of a finite sample space, with event probabilities obtained by summing outcome probabilities.
required_concepts: A finite probability space assigns nonnegative probabilities summing to one to the outcomes of a finite sample space
with event probabilities obtained by summing outcome probabilities.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all outcomes are equally likely without that model assumption.

cards.prompt: Define Finite random variable. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** On a finite probability space (Omega,P), a real-valued random variable is a function X:Omega->R; its randomness comes from the sampled outcome, not from the function rule changing.
required_concepts: A finite random variable is a function X:Omega->R on a finite probability space.
The sampled outcome is random; X is a fixed function of that outcome.
major_error_concepts: Treating a random variable as an event or as a rule that changes randomly after the outcome is sampled.

cards.prompt: What is the finite union bound used for, and what is its limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The union bound controls the chance that at least one bad event occurs using only marginal probabilities; it can be loose when events overlap heavily.
required_concepts: It upper-bounds the probability that at least one bad event occurs using marginal probabilities.
It may be loose when events overlap heavily.
major_error_concepts: Treating the upper bound as the exact union probability when events overlap.

cards.prompt: State the finite union bound and its assumptions.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For events A_1,...,A_m in a finite probability space, P(union_i A_i)<=sum_i P(A_i); no independence assumption is required.
required_concepts: The event family is finite.
P(union_i A_i)<=sum_i P(A_i).
No independence assumption is required.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the inequality by equality for overlapping events or requiring independence.

cards.prompt: Define first-moment method. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For a nonnegative integer-valued X, P(X>=1)<=E[X]; hence E[X]<1 implies that an outcome with X=0 exists.
required_concepts: For a nonnegative integer-valued X, P(X>=1)<=E[X]; hence E[X]<1 implies that an outcome with X=0 exists.
major_error_concepts: Inferring P(X=0)>0 from E[X]<1 when X can take negative or noninteger values.

cards.prompt: Define generating-function product. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The coefficient of x^n in A(x)B(x) is the convolution sum sum_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n-k}, encoding paired constructions whose sizes add to n.
required_concepts: The coefficient of x^n in A(x)B(x) is the convolution sum sum_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n-k}, encoding paired constructions whose sizes add to n.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying coefficients termwise instead of convolving them.

cards.prompt: Define graph cut. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** In an undirected graph, for S subseteq V the cut delta(S) is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S and one in V\S. Directed graphs require separate out-cut and in-cut conventions.
required_concepts: For an undirected graph, delta(S) contains exactly edges with one endpoint in S and one in V\S.
Directed graphs require distinct in-cut and out-cut conventions.
major_error_concepts: Calling an arbitrary edge subset a cut, or using the undirected exactly-one-endpoint formula without distinguishing directed in-cuts and out-cuts.

cards.prompt: Define graph distance. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The distance between two connected vertices is the minimum number of edges in a path joining them; it is infinite or undefined by convention across components.
required_concepts: The distance between two connected vertices is the minimum number of edges in a path joining them; it is infinite or undefined by convention across components.
major_error_concepts: Using the length of an arbitrary path rather than the minimum path length, or assigning a finite distance across components.

cards.prompt: Define graph isomorphism. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A graph isomorphism from G to H is a vertex bijection phi such that an edge joins u and v in G if and only if the corresponding edge joins phi(u) and phi(v) in H, with direction, multiplicity, and labels preserved when they belong to the graph structure.
required_concepts: The vertex map is a bijection.
Adjacency and nonadjacency are preserved in both directions, along with any declared direction, multiplicity, or labels.
major_error_concepts: Using a nonbijective vertex map, or preserving degree counts while failing to preserve adjacency in both directions.

cards.prompt: What is Hall's marriage theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** Hall's theorem characterizes when a bipartite matching saturating a designated finite left part exists and exposes deficient subsets as the obstruction; it establishes existence, not uniqueness of the matching.
required_concepts: Hall's theorem characterizes when a bipartite matching can saturate the designated left part.
A subset with fewer neighbors than vertices is the exact obstruction, not evidence about uniqueness.
major_error_concepts: Claiming Hall's condition produces a unique matching.

cards.prompt: State Hall's marriage theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** A finite bipartite graph with parts X and Y has a matching saturating X exactly when every S subseteq X satisfies |N(S)|>=|S|, where N(S)={y in Y: some x in S is adjacent to y}.
required_concepts: The graph is finite and bipartite with declared parts X and Y.
For S subseteq X, N(S) is the set of vertices in Y adjacent to at least one x in S.
A matching saturating X exists exactly when |N(S)|>=|S| for every S subseteq X.
major_error_concepts: Checking the neighborhood condition only for single vertices instead of every subset of X.

cards.prompt: How do a Hamilton path and a Hamilton cycle differ?
cards.definition: **Definition.** A Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once; a Hamilton cycle returns to its start after visiting every other vertex exactly once.
required_concepts: A Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once.
A Hamilton cycle is a cycle containing every vertex exactly once apart from the repeated start/end vertex.
major_error_concepts: Using Euler degree conditions as a general criterion for Hamilton paths.

cards.prompt: What is handshaking lemma used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It changes a vertex-degree sum into an edge count and yields parity facts such as the even number of odd-degree vertices; its undirected form cannot be reused unchanged for directed degrees.
required_concepts: It changes a vertex-degree sum into an edge count and yields parity facts such as the even number of odd-degree vertices
its undirected form cannot be reused unchanged for directed degrees.
major_error_concepts: Applying the undirected degree identity to a directed graph without replacing it by in-degree and out-degree sums.

cards.prompt: State handshaking lemma, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For every finite undirected graph, the sum of vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges; consequently, the number of odd-degree vertices is even.
required_concepts: For every finite undirected graph, the sum of vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges
consequently, the number of odd-degree vertices is even.
major_error_concepts: Applying the undirected degree identity to a directed graph without replacing it by in-degree and out-degree sums.

cards.prompt: Define Hasse diagram. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A Hasse diagram represents a finite poset by drawing cover relations upward and omitting reflexive and transitively implied edges.
required_concepts: A Hasse diagram represents a finite poset by drawing cover relations upward and omitting reflexive and transitively implied edges.
major_error_concepts: Retaining every reflexive and transitive comparison produces a relation diagram, not the transitive-reduction convention of a Hasse diagram.

cards.prompt: Define homogeneous linear recurrence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A homogeneous linear recurrence has zero forcing term, so every term is a linear combination only of earlier sequence terms.
required_concepts: A homogeneous linear recurrence has zero forcing term, so every term is a linear combination only of earlier sequence terms.
major_error_concepts: Calling a recurrence homogeneous because its coefficients are constant while a nonzero forcing term remains.

cards.prompt: How does a solution of a linear nonhomogeneous recurrence decompose into particular and homogeneous parts?
cards.definition: **Definition.** For a linear nonhomogeneous recurrence, fix one particular solution of that recurrence. Every solution is that fixed particular solution plus an arbitrary solution of the associated homogeneous recurrence; initial conditions then determine the homogeneous coefficients.
required_concepts: Subtracting a particular solution leaves a solution of the associated homogeneous recurrence.
Every solution equals one particular solution plus an arbitrary homogeneous solution.
Initial conditions determine the remaining homogeneous coefficients.
major_error_concepts: Treating one particular solution as the full solution or forgetting to add the associated homogeneous family before imposing initial conditions.

cards.prompt: What is the constant-coefficient homogeneous recurrence solution theorem used for, and what is its boundary?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The theorem converts a recurrence into a finite basis of exponential-polynomial sequences and makes repeated-root multiplicity load-bearing; it does not directly cover variable coefficients or a nonzero forcing term.
required_concepts: It turns the recurrence into an exponential-polynomial solution basis.
Repeated roots require polynomial factors in n.
The theorem does not directly handle variable coefficients or nonzero forcing terms.
major_error_concepts: Applying the characteristic-root basis unchanged to a variable-coefficient or nonhomogeneous recurrence.

cards.prompt: State the characteristic-root solution theorem for a constant-coefficient homogeneous recurrence, including repeated roots.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For a homogeneous linear recurrence of order k with constant coefficients and characteristic roots r_1,...,r_s of multiplicities m_1,...,m_s over C, every solution has the form sum_i P_i(n) r_i^n with degree P_i<m_i, and the k coefficients are uniquely determined by k consecutive initial values.
required_concepts: The recurrence is homogeneous, linear, order k, and has constant coefficients.
A root r_i of multiplicity m_i contributes P_i(n)r_i^n with degree P_i<m_i.
The full solution is the sum of those contributions.
K consecutive initial values uniquely determine the k scalar coefficients.
major_error_concepts: Using only c r^n for a repeated root of multiplicity greater than one, or omitting the initial values needed to determine the coefficients.

cards.prompt: What is principle of inclusion-exclusion used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** Inclusion-exclusion gives an exact finite-union count by alternating corrections for all nonempty intersections; the full formula may require exponentially many terms.
required_concepts: It corrects repeated counting caused by overlapping properties.
Its standard uses include exact union counts, derangements, and finite sieve arguments.
The full n-set formula may require 2^n-1 intersection terms.
major_error_concepts: Using it as an independence assumption rather than an exact finite identity.

cards.prompt: State principle of inclusion-exclusion, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For finite sets A1,...,An, the size of their union is the alternating sum over all nonempty index sets I of (-1)^{|I|+1} times the size of the intersection of Ai for i in I.
required_concepts: The family A_1,...,A_n is finite and every A_i is finite.
The union size is sum over every nonempty I subseteq {1,...,n} of (-1)^{|I|+1}|intersection_{i in I} A_i|.
major_error_concepts: Adding pairwise corrections but omitting higher intersections when more than two sets are present.

cards.prompt: How do indegree and outdegree differ, and how does a loop contribute to them?
cards.definition: **Definition.** In a directed graph, indegree counts incoming edges and outdegree counts outgoing edges, with loops contributing to both.
required_concepts: Indegree counts incoming edge ends and outdegree counts outgoing edge ends.
A directed loop contributes one to both indegree and outdegree.
major_error_concepts: Counting every incident directed edge in both degrees, except for loops which legitimately contribute once to each.

cards.prompt: Define independent set. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** An independent set is a vertex subset containing no adjacent pair.
required_concepts: An independent set is a vertex subset containing no adjacent pair.
major_error_concepts: Confusing independent sets with probabilistically independent events.

cards.prompt: Define induced subgraph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The subgraph induced by a vertex subset contains exactly those original edges whose endpoints both lie in the subset.
required_concepts: The subgraph induced by a vertex subset contains exactly those original edges whose endpoints both lie in the subset.
major_error_concepts: Selecting a vertex subset but arbitrarily dropping an original edge whose two endpoints both remain.

cards.prompt: Define integer partition. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** An integer partition of n is a multiset of positive integers whose sum is n, conventionally represented in nonincreasing order.
required_concepts: An integer partition of n is a multiset of positive integers whose sum is n, conventionally represented in nonincreasing order.
major_error_concepts: Treating different orders of the same parts as different partitions.

cards.prompt: Define lattice. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A lattice is a poset in which every pair has both a least upper bound (join) and a greatest lower bound (meet).
required_concepts: A lattice is a poset in which every pair has both a least upper bound (join) and a greatest lower bound (meet).
major_error_concepts: Claiming every poset is a lattice, or accepting a pair with no least upper bound or no greatest lower bound.

cards.prompt: Define linear extension. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A linear extension of a partial order is a total order on the same set that preserves every original comparison.
required_concepts: A linear extension of a partial order is a total order on the same set that preserves every original comparison.
major_error_concepts: Reversing a comparable pair from the partial order, or ordering a different ground set.

cards.prompt: Define linear recurrence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A linear recurrence expresses each sequence term as a linear combination of specified earlier terms plus an optional forcing term.
required_concepts: A linear recurrence expresses each sequence term as a linear combination of specified earlier terms plus an optional forcing term.
major_error_concepts: Calling a recurrence linear when products or nonlinear functions of earlier terms appear.

cards.prompt: Define finite-structure logical equivalence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Two claims about a declared finite structure are logically equivalent when they agree under every admissible assignment or interpretation of that structure; finite checking is sound only when it exhausts the declared possibilities.
required_concepts: The two claims agree under every admissible assignment or interpretation of the declared finite structure.
A finite truth check establishes equivalence only when it exhausts all admissible cases.
major_error_concepts: Calling two finite-structure claims equivalent after checking only a few assignments rather than all admissible cases.

cards.prompt: Define loop invariant. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A loop invariant is a proposition about program state that holds before the first iteration and is preserved by every iteration; if the loop terminates, it holds on exit, but preservation alone does not prove termination.
required_concepts: The invariant holds before the first iteration.
Every iteration preserves it.
If the loop terminates, the invariant holds on exit.
Invariant preservation alone does not prove termination.
major_error_concepts: Proving preservation without initialization, or claiming the invariant itself establishes that the loop terminates.

cards.prompt: What is symmetric Lovasz local lemma: role used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The local lemma proves simultaneous avoidance when each bad event has limited dependency, even when a union bound is too weak; it is an existence result unless paired with a constructive method.
required_concepts: The local lemma proves simultaneous avoidance when each bad event has limited dependency, even when a union bound is too weak
it is an existence result unless paired with a constructive method.
major_error_concepts: Treating the existential local-lemma conclusion as an efficient sampler or repair algorithm without an additional constructive result.

cards.prompt: State symmetric Lovasz local lemma: statement, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** Let A_i be finitely many events with P(A_i)<=p and a dependency graph of maximum degree d, so each event is independent of the joint collection of its nonneighbors. If e p(d+1)<=1, then P(intersection_i A_i^c)>0.
required_concepts: The finitely many bad events have probabilities at most p and a dependency graph of maximum degree d.
Each event is independent of the joint collection indexed by its nonneighbors.
The numerical condition e p(d+1)<=1 implies positive probability that no bad event occurs.
major_error_concepts: Using only small marginal probabilities while ignoring the dependency-graph condition, or reversing the conclusion into independence of the bad events.

cards.prompt: What is master theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The Master theorem classifies balanced equal-size divide-and-conquer recurrences by comparing branching work with nonrecursive work; it does not cover arbitrary recurrences, unequal subproblem sizes, or functions falling into its case gaps.
required_concepts: It classifies balanced equal-size divide-and-conquer recurrences by comparing branching and nonrecursive work.
It does not cover arbitrary recurrences, unequal subproblem sizes, or functions outside its three case hypotheses.
major_error_concepts: Treating it as a solver for arbitrary recurrences, unequal subproblem sizes, or oscillatory forcing terms.

cards.prompt: State master theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** Let a>=1 and b>1 be constants, let f:N->R_{>=0}, and let T:N->R_{>=0} satisfy T(n)=aT(floor(n/b))+f(n) for all sufficiently large integers n with T(n)=Theta(1) below a fixed threshold. Put c=log_b(a). If f(n)=O(n^{c-epsilon}) for some epsilon>0, then T(n)=Theta(n^c). If f(n)=Theta(n^c log^k n) for some k>=0, then T(n)=Theta(n^c log^{k+1} n). If f(n)=Omega(n^{c+epsilon}) for some epsilon>0 and a f(floor(n/b))<=q f(n) eventually for some q<1, then T(n)=Theta(f(n)).
required_concepts: The recurrence is T(n)=aT(floor(n/b))+f(n) for sufficiently large integers n, with constants a>=1, b>1, nonnegative f, and Theta(1) base values below a fixed threshold.
With c=log_b(a), f(n)=O(n^{c-epsilon}) for some epsilon>0 implies T(n)=Theta(n^c).
If f(n)=Theta(n^c log^k n) for k>=0, then T(n)=Theta(n^c log^{k+1} n).
If f(n)=Omega(n^{c+epsilon}) and a f(floor(n/b))<=q f(n) eventually for some q<1, then T(n)=Theta(f(n)).
major_error_concepts: Applying the theorem without matching an admissible case or checking the regularity condition in the larger-f case.

cards.prompt: Define matching. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A matching is a set of edges no two of which share a vertex.
required_concepts: A matching is a set of edges no two of which share a vertex.
major_error_concepts: Allowing a vertex to be incident to two selected matching edges.

cards.prompt: Define multinomial coefficient. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For nonnegative k_1+...+k_m=n, the multinomial coefficient n!/(k_1!...k_m!) counts words or allocations with category multiplicities k_1,...,k_m.
required_concepts: For nonnegative k_1+...+k_m=n, the multinomial coefficient n!/(k_1!...k_m!) counts words or allocations with category multiplicities k_1,...,k_m.
major_error_concepts: Using n!/(k_1!...k_m!) when the nonnegative multiplicities do not sum to n.

cards.prompt: Define ordinary generating function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The ordinary generating function of a sequence (a_n) is the formal power series A(x)=sum_{n>=0} a_n x^n.
required_concepts: The ordinary generating function of a sequence (a_n) is the formal power series A(x)=sum_{n>=0} a_n x^n.
major_error_concepts: Treating a formal generating function as an analytically convergent function without checking convergence.

cards.prompt: Define perfect matching. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A perfect matching is a matching that covers every vertex of the graph.
required_concepts: A perfect matching is a matching that covers every vertex of the graph.
major_error_concepts: Calling a maximal matching perfect when it leaves vertices unmatched.

cards.prompt: Define permutation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A permutation of an n-element set is a bijection from the set to itself; equivalently, a linear arrangement of its n distinct elements, of which there are n!.
required_concepts: A permutation is a bijection of a set with itself, equivalently a linear arrangement of distinct elements.
An n-element set has n! permutations.
major_error_concepts: Using n! when repetitions or indistinguishable objects change the counting object.

cards.prompt: Define permutations of a multiset. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A multiset with n total objects and multiplicities k_1,...,k_m has n!/(k_1!...k_m!) distinct linear arrangements.
required_concepts: A multiset with n total objects and multiplicities k_1,...,k_m has n!/(k_1!...k_m!) distinct linear arrangements.
major_error_concepts: Counting copies of the same repeated value as distinguishable and reporting n! arrangements.

cards.prompt: What is pigeonhole principle used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The pigeonhole principle proves that some box has a collision or concentration when avoidance would make total capacity too small; it need not identify which box.
required_concepts: It proves existence by comparing the number of objects with total avoidance capacity.
It need not identify the crowded box.
major_error_concepts: Claiming it identifies which particular box must be crowded when only existence is established.

cards.prompt: State pigeonhole principle, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** If N objects are assigned to k boxes, where N is a nonnegative integer and k is a positive integer, some box receives at least ceil(N/k) objects; in particular, N>k forces a box containing at least two objects.
required_concepts: All N objects are assigned among a positive number k of boxes.
Some box contains at least ceil(N/k) objects.
The special case N>k forces at least two objects in one box.
major_error_concepts: Using floor(N/k) as the forced lower bound or omitting that every object is assigned to a box.

cards.prompt: Define planar embedding. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A planar embedding maps vertices to distinct points of the plane and edges to arcs whose interiors are pairwise disjoint and contain no nonincident vertex.
required_concepts: Vertices map to distinct points and edges to endpoint-preserving arcs.
Edge interiors are pairwise disjoint and contain no nonincident vertex.
major_error_concepts: Calling a drawing an embedding when two edge interiors cross or a vertex lies in a nonincident edge's interior.

cards.prompt: Define planar graph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A planar graph admits a drawing in the plane with no edge crossings except at common endpoints.
required_concepts: A planar graph admits a drawing in the plane with no edge crossings except at common endpoints.
major_error_concepts: Declaring a graph nonplanar because one particular drawing has crossings.

cards.prompt: Define partially ordered set. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A partially ordered set is a pair (P, <=) consisting of a set and a specified partial order on it.
required_concepts: A partially ordered set is a pair (P, <=) consisting of a set and a specified partial order on it.
major_error_concepts: Referring to a set as ordered without identifying the relation.

cards.prompt: What is the reusable proof idea behind probabilistic method?
cards.definition: **Definition.** The probabilistic method proves that a combinatorial object exists by defining a random object and showing the desired property has positive probability.
required_concepts: The probabilistic method proves that a combinatorial object exists by defining a random object and showing the desired property has positive probability.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the method samples the desired object efficiently merely because existence probability is positive.

cards.prompt: Define Combinatorial product rule. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** If a construction has k successive stages and stage i offers n_i choices for every admissible history of earlier choices, then it has product_i n_i complete choice sequences.
required_concepts: The construction has successive stages.
At stage i, every admissible earlier history has exactly n_i choices.
The number of complete choice sequences is product_i n_i.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying nominal stage counts when the number of later choices varies with the earlier history.

cards.prompt: Define finite combinatorial proposition. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A finite combinatorial proposition is a closed truth-valued claim about a declared finite structure, obtained after importing the general proposition and variable-binding language from Mathematical Proof and Foundations.
required_concepts: The claim is closed and truth-valued.
Its objects and interpretation belong to a declared finite structure.
major_error_concepts: Treating an open sentence about a graph or finite set as a proposition before its variables are assigned or quantified.

cards.prompt: Define finite-structure quantifier order. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** In a finite structure, quantifier order controls witness dependence: forall x exists y P(x,y) may choose a different y for each x, whereas exists y forall x P(x,y) requires one y that works for every x.
required_concepts: In forall x exists y P(x,y), the witness y may depend on x.
In exists y forall x P(x,y), one witness y must work for every x.
The two claims are not equivalent in general.
major_error_concepts: Swapping universal and existential quantifiers without changing the claim.

cards.prompt: Define random construction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A random construction is the explicit specification of the finite object space and probability distribution to which a probabilistic existence argument is applied.
required_concepts: Declare the finite combinatorial object space.
Declare the probability law used to sample it.
This construction supplies the model; the probabilistic method supplies the existence inference.
major_error_concepts: Saying 'choose randomly' without declaring the object space and probability law.

cards.prompt: Define Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n,p). Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** In G(n,p), the vertex set has size n and each possible undirected edge is included independently with probability p.
required_concepts: In G(n,p), the vertex set has size n and each possible undirected edge is included independently with probability p.
major_error_concepts: Confusing G(n,p) with the model having exactly a fixed number of edges.

cards.prompt: Define recurrence relation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A recurrence relation constrains each term of a sequence using earlier terms, together with enough initial conditions to determine the intended sequence.
required_concepts: A recurrence relation constrains each term of a sequence using earlier terms, together with enough initial conditions to determine the intended sequence.
major_error_concepts: Writing a recurrence without initial conditions and claiming it defines a unique sequence.

cards.prompt: Define simple graph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A simple undirected graph has edges that are unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no loops and no parallel edges.
required_concepts: A simple undirected graph has edges that are unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no loops and no parallel edges.
major_error_concepts: Calling a graph simple while allowing a loop or repeated edge.

cards.prompt: What is simple planar edge bound: role used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The edge bound is a fast necessary test for planarity derived from minimum face length; it is not a planarity characterization.
required_concepts: The edge bound is a fast necessary test for planarity derived from minimum face length
it is not a planarity characterization.
major_error_concepts: Concluding that a graph is planar merely because it satisfies the edge inequality.

cards.prompt: State simple planar edge bound: statement, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** Every simple connected planar graph with V>=3 satisfies E<=3V-6; if it is also bipartite, E<=2V-4.
required_concepts: Every simple connected planar graph with V>=3 satisfies E<=3V-6
if it is also bipartite, E<=2V-4.
major_error_concepts: Applying E<=3V-6 to a multigraph with two-edge faces, or applying the bipartite improvement without bipartiteness.

cards.prompt: Define spanning tree. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A spanning tree of a connected graph is a subgraph containing every vertex and forming a tree.
required_concepts: A spanning tree of a connected graph is a subgraph containing every vertex and forming a tree.
major_error_concepts: Calling a tree on only a subset of vertices spanning.

cards.prompt: What is stars-and-bars theorem: role used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** Stars and bars converts indistinguishable allocations into separator positions; upper bounds or other side constraints require inclusion-exclusion or another method.
required_concepts: Stars and bars converts indistinguishable allocations into separator positions
upper bounds or other side constraints require inclusion-exclusion or another method.
major_error_concepts: Applying stars and bars when objects are distinguishable or when upper bounds invalidate the unrestricted occupancy model.

cards.prompt: State stars-and-bars theorem: statement, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For integers k>=1 and n>=0, the number of nonnegative integer solutions to x_1+...+x_k=n is binom(n+k-1,k-1); when n>=k, the number of positive integer solutions is binom(n-1,k-1).
required_concepts: For k>=1 and n>=0, nonnegative solutions are counted by binom(n+k-1,k-1).
For n>=k, positive solutions are counted by binom(n-1,k-1).
major_error_concepts: Using the nonnegative-solution formula for positive parts without shifting each variable by one, or applying either formula outside its integer hypotheses.

cards.prompt: What is the reusable strong-induction pattern for a discrete decomposition argument?
cards.definition: **Definition.** In discrete decomposition arguments, strong induction proves P(n) by reducing an object of size n to one or more strictly smaller sizes and applying the imported strong-induction hypothesis to those components.
required_concepts: Reduce the size-n object to one or more objects of strictly smaller size.
Apply the imported strong-induction hypothesis to the smaller components.
Recombine the component conclusions to prove P(n).
major_error_concepts: Applying the induction hypothesis to a component that is not strictly smaller makes the decomposition argument circular.

cards.prompt: Define subgraph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For finite graphs H and G under the same graph convention, H is a subgraph of G when V(H) is a subset of V(G), E(H) is a subset of E(G), and every edge of H retains its incidence from G. A subgraph may omit vertices and edges.
required_concepts: V(H) is a subset of V(G) and E(H) is a subset of E(G).
Every edge retained in H keeps its incidence from G.
A subgraph may omit vertices and edges and need not be induced.
major_error_concepts: Calling H a subgraph while adding a vertex or edge absent from G, changing an edge's incidence, or requiring every subgraph to be induced.

cards.prompt: Define sum rule. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** If a choice can be made from pairwise disjoint alternatives of sizes n1,...,nk, the total number of choices is n1+...+nk.
required_concepts: If a choice can be made from pairwise disjoint alternatives of sizes n1,...,nk, the total number of choices is n1+...+nk.
major_error_concepts: Adding counts of overlapping alternatives without correcting the overlap.

cards.prompt: What is topological-order characterization: role used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The characterization turns finite dependency feasibility into directed-cycle detection and supports source-removal induction; it applies to directed, not merely undirected, acyclicity.
required_concepts: It turns finite dependency feasibility into directed-cycle detection.
It supports source-removal induction or a topological-sort algorithm.
The relevant obstruction is a directed cycle, not merely an undirected cycle.
major_error_concepts: Treating one failed ordering attempt as proof of a cycle instead of using a valid source-removal or cycle-detection argument.

cards.prompt: State topological-order characterization: statement, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** A finite directed graph has a topological ordering if and only if it is acyclic.
required_concepts: A finite directed graph has a topological ordering if and only if it is acyclic.
major_error_concepts: Claiming that a directed graph containing a directed cycle has a topological ordering, or dropping the finiteness hypothesis from this formulation.

cards.prompt: Define topological ordering. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A topological ordering of a directed graph is a linear order placing every edge's tail before its head.
required_concepts: A topological ordering of a directed graph is a linear order placing every edge's tail before its head.
major_error_concepts: Placing an edge head before its tail, or calling an ordering of only some vertices topological.

cards.prompt: What is finite tree characterizations used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It lets a proof establish that a finite graph is a tree by verifying any suitable two of connectedness, acyclicity, and the n-minus-one edge count, and it supports switching to the unique-path characterization; one condition alone is not enough.
required_concepts: It lets a proof establish that a finite graph is a tree by verifying any suitable two of connectedness, acyclicity, and the n-minus-one edge count, and it supports switching to the unique-path characterization
one condition alone is not enough.
major_error_concepts: Using the n-1 edge condition alone to conclude the graph is a tree.

cards.prompt: State finite tree characterizations, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For a nonempty finite undirected graph with n>=1 vertices, any two of connectedness, acyclicity, and having n-1 edges imply the third; equivalently, it is a tree exactly when every two vertices are joined by a unique path.
required_concepts: The graph is finite, undirected, and nonempty, with n>=1 vertices.
Any two of connectedness, acyclicity, and having n-1 edges imply the third.
Equivalently, a tree has a unique path between every pair of vertices.
major_error_concepts: Using the n-1 edge condition alone to conclude the graph is a tree.

cards.prompt: Define tree. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A tree is a connected simple undirected graph containing no cycle.
required_concepts: The graph is simple and undirected.
It is connected and contains no cycle.
major_error_concepts: Calling every acyclic graph a tree rather than a forest when it is disconnected.

cards.term: universal quantification over a finite structure
cards.prompt: Define universal quantification over a finite structure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** For a declared finite domain D, forall x in D, P(x) asserts P(x) for every member of D and can be checked by an exhaustive traversal of D.
required_concepts: The quantifier ranges over every member of the declared finite domain D.
Exhaustive traversal is a valid check because D is finite and fully specified.
major_error_concepts: Refuting a universal claim without producing an element in its domain for which the predicate is false.

cards.prompt: Define proper vertex coloring. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A proper vertex coloring assigns colors to vertices so adjacent vertices receive different colors.
required_concepts: A proper vertex coloring assigns colors to vertices so adjacent vertices receive different colors.
major_error_concepts: Treating color labels as ordered numerical values rather than interchangeable categories.

cards.prompt: Define vertex degree. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** In an undirected graph, the degree of a vertex is the number of incident edge ends, counting a loop twice when loops are allowed.
required_concepts: In an undirected graph, the degree of a vertex is the number of incident edge ends, counting a loop twice when loops are allowed.
major_error_concepts: Counting a loop once in the undirected degree sum.

cards.prompt: Distinguish walk, trail, and path.
cards.definition: **Definition.** In an undirected graph, a walk is a vertex-edge sequence in which each edge joins its consecutive vertices; a trail is an undirected walk with no repeated edge, and a path is an undirected walk with no repeated vertex. Directed traversal is a later convention and must respect arc orientation.
required_concepts: The card's walk, trail, and path are undirected graph notions.
An undirected walk has consecutive vertices joined by the intervening edge.
An undirected trail repeats no edge.
An undirected path repeats no vertex.
A later directed traversal must respect arc orientation.
major_error_concepts: Using walk, trail, and path as synonyms, losing their distinct repetition constraints, or applying the undirected incidence convention to a directed arc without respecting its orientation.

cards.prompt: How do weak and positive compositions differ, and how do both differ from an integer partition?
cards.definition: **Definition.** A weak composition of n into k parts is an ordered k-tuple of nonnegative integers summing to n, while a positive composition requires every part to be positive. Both are ordered tuples, unlike an integer partition, which is unordered.
required_concepts: A weak composition permits zero parts.
A positive composition requires every part to be positive.
Both are ordered tuples, unlike integer partitions.
major_error_concepts: Treating zero parts as admissible in a positive composition, or treating the ordered parts as an unordered integer partition.

cards.prompt: Define well-founded recursion. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** Well-founded recursion defines an object's value from values at strictly smaller predecessors under a well-founded relation.
required_concepts: Well-founded recursion defines an object's value from values at strictly smaller predecessors under a well-founded relation.
major_error_concepts: Allowing a recursive dependency that does not decrease in the declared well-founded relation.

cards.prompt: Define well-founded relation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A relation R on A is well-founded when every nonempty subset S of A has an R-minimal element m in S: no s in S satisfies s R m.
required_concepts: Every nonempty subset S of A has an R-minimal element m in S.
R-minimal means that no s in S satisfies s R m.
major_error_concepts: Calling a relation well-founded merely because it is transitive, or checking for a minimal element only in A rather than in every nonempty subset of A.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Discrete Mathematics.
